To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

collaborative inhibition is obtained for both younger (Experiment 1, free report cued recall; Experiment 2, free recall) and older (Experiment 1 and 2, free report cuded recall; Experiment 1, free recall) adults on initial tests and does not persist on subsequent tests.

collaborative inhibition is obtained for both younger adults and older adults across repeated retrieval attempts, and that the magnitude of false alarms is exaggerated for older adults after a free recall collaborative condition.

collaborative inhibition is found in older adults, but only when they are tested on a free recall test, not when tested on a cued recall test, and that the effects of collaborative inhibition on false alarms on a recognition test are greater for older adults than younger adults.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of collaboration on recall.
the role of retrieval in the development of collaborative inhibition.
the effects of collaborative memory on older and younger adults’ memory performance.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
collaborative inhibition is not a function of the type of retrieval instruction (free report vs. forced report) and is not affected by age.
collaborative inhibition is a robust phenomenon and that the age differences in collaborative memory are not due to the effect of collaborative inhibition per se.
the effect is robust across age, retrieval manipulation, and test, but that the magnitude is affected by the retrieval manipulations and the test type.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
older adults’ memory for information is more susceptible to disruption from social interactions than is younger adults’ memory.
collaborative inhibition is an important phenomenon that can be explained by strategy disruption and source memory, and it may be exacerbated in older adults.
older adults are more susceptible to collaborative inhibition than are younger adults.
The main takeaway from our work is that
collaborative inhibition can be used to study memory processes in older adults.
the effects of collaboration on recall and false memory are similar for younger and older adults, and that these effects can be explained in a common framework.
collaborative inhibition does not persist across repeated retrieval attempts, and this finding is consistent across both free recall and cued recall tasks.
